sermon:
## What the Locust Left
*When the harvest is gone and so is the noise we hid behind*

**Text:** Joel 1:1-20 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 28:38-42 · Amos 4:9 · Lamentations 2:11 · Psalm 137:1

The field is bare. The vines are stripped. The priests who should be leading worship are standing in an empty sanctuary with nothing to put on the altar, and a prophet looks at the wreckage and refuses to call it bad weather.

We want our disasters to be accidents. An accident asks nothing of us.

**The Loss That Outlives Memory**
Joel begins not with an explanation but with a command to remember. "Hear this, you elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the land. Has such a thing happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation." (Joel 1:2-3) Four generations of locusts: "What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten. What the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten, and what the hopping locust left, the destroying locust has eaten." (Joel 1:4) This is not one bad season. It is the slow, total stripping of everything a people built a life on. Moses had warned an agricultural nation exactly here, "You shall carry much seed into the field and shall gather little in, for the locust shall consume it." (Deuteronomy 28:38) Amos had said it again over a deaf people: "I laid waste your gardens and your vineyards; your fig trees and your olive trees the locust devoured; yet you did not return to me." (Amos 4:9) The horror in Joel is not that locusts came. It is that nothing was left, and the people still had not understood what the loss was for.

We are good at this. We absorb the loss, we file the insurance claim, we rebuild the barn, and we never once ask the question the bare field is asking us.

**The Silence Where the Worship Used to Be**
Joel turns to the people who lived loudest and makes them the first to weep. "Awake, you drunkards, and weep, and wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it is cut off from your mouth." (Joel 1:5) The numbing agent is gone. Then the prophet does something that should stop every churchgoer cold, he aims the grief at the altar. "The grain offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the LORD. The priests mourn, the ministers of the LORD." (Joel 1:9) When the locust ate the grain and dried the vine, it did not only empty the table. It emptied the worship. There was nothing left to bring to God. The fast was not chosen. It was imposed by ruin. "The fields are destroyed, the ground mourns, because the grain is destroyed, the wine dries up, the oil languishes." (Joel 1:10) This is what loss does that we rarely name aloud, it reaches all the way into the sanctuary and stops the offering. The same ache runs under the exile, when those who once led the songs sat down by foreign rivers: "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land?" (Psalm 137:4) Devastation total enough to silence the wine is total enough to silence the praise, and Joel will not let the priests pretend otherwise.

I have stood in the empty space where worship used to be and called my silence a season instead of a summons. I have let a loss reorganize my whole life and never once asked what God was saying through it. That is the danger the prophet is naming. Not that the field is bare. That the bare field speaks, and we have trained ourselves not to hear it.

**The First Faithful Act Is a Cry**
Notice what Joel does not do. He does not explain the locusts. He does not assign the blame, build the recovery plan, or rush to comfort. He commands a gathering, and the gathering is for grief. "Put on sackcloth and lament, O priests; wail, O ministers of the altar... Consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly. Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land to the house of the LORD your God, and cry out to the LORD." (Joel 1:13-14) Before there is a single word of hope in this book, there is an assembly summoned to weep. And then the prophet does what he is telling them to do. He does not stay above the grief, managing it. He enters it: "To you, O LORD, I call. For fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has burned all the trees of the field. Even the beasts of the field pant for you because the water brooks are dried up." (Joel 1:19-20) The man who saw God's hand in the ruin is the same man on his face crying out to that God. This is the order Scripture insists on and we keep reversing. Not explanation, then maybe lament. Lament first. The prophet who wept over a ruined city, "my eyes are spent with weeping... because infants and babies faint in the streets" (Lamentations 2:11), knew the same thing Joel knows. Before the field is restored, the field must be mourned. The locust is not the enemy of faith here. The hurry past the grief is.

And this is where a church two and a half millennia later finally hears its own name. We are an expert people at absorbing loss without ever crying out. We medicate the ache, schedule around the empty altar, and call the numbness peace. Joel's whole first chapter is the prophetic refusal to let us do that, and it ends not with an answer but with a man on the ground, calling to the only One who can do anything about it. The gospel does not skip this room. The Lord who would one day weep at a tomb, and sweat in a garden, and cry out from a cross, did not float above human grief. He went down into it. The Day the prophet is about to announce will not come around the lament. It will come through it.

Wake up and grieve before God.

## Return to Me
*The day no strength survives, and the one door God leaves open*

**Text:** Joel 2:1-17 · **Supporting:** Zephaniah 1:14-15 · Exodus 34:6 · Jonah 4:2 · Hosea 6:1

A trumpet on the city wall meant one thing in the ancient world. Enemy in sight. Get up, get armed, get ready. Joel blows it, and tells the people there is nothing to arm against, because the army marching is the one no wall has ever held.

**The Day No One Outruns**
Joel takes the locust plague of chapter one and turns it into a window onto something far larger. "Blow a trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm on my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD is coming; it is near." (Joel 2:1) Then the army: "a great and powerful people; their like has never been before, nor will be again after them through the years of all generations." (Joel 2:2) They scale walls, they march in column, they do not break ranks, and the earth quakes before them. The locusts were a preview. The Day of the LORD is the reality they were pointing at. And the prophet refuses to soften what that Day is, "The day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joel 2:11) Zephaniah, prophesying in the same vein, called it exactly what it is: "A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish, a day of ruin and devastation, a day of darkness and gloom." (Zephaniah 1:15) This is the thing modern religion has quietly deleted. We have kept a God who is useful and lost a God who is dangerous. Joel will not let the deletion stand. There is a Day, it is coming, it is near, and no human strength survives it.

We have built a faith almost entirely around what God can do for us. Joel is announcing a God we will one day stand before, and that is a different God than the one most of us pray to.

**The One Door God Names Himself**
And then, in the middle of an army no one survives, comes the most astonishing word in the book. "Yet even now," declares the LORD. (Joel 2:12) Even now, with the trumpet sounding, the Day near, the case closed, there is a door, and God himself holds it open. But notice who opens it. The people do not invent the way back. God names it. "Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning." (Joel 2:12) The only road out of the Day is the one God draws, and it leads straight back to him. Then the line that exposes every religion we have ever manufactured: "and rend your hearts and not your garments." (Joel 2:13) Tearing your clothes was the visible, public, respectable sign of grief. You could do it and feel the matter handled. God refuses the performance and demands the heart. He is not asking for a display. He is asking for the actual man underneath the torn shirt.

I have torn the garment and kept the heart whole. I have led the public grief and gone home unchanged. I have stood in the place of the priest and produced the sign of repentance without the substance of it, and done it well enough that no one knew. That is the precise thing Joel is naming. Not the absence of religion. The presence of religion with the heart left out.

**Who He Is on the Other Side of the Door**
Why would anyone tear the heart open before a God like this? Joel answers, and his answer is the oldest creed in Scripture. "Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster." (Joel 2:13) That is not Joel's invention. It is the self-revelation God gave Moses on the mountain after the golden calf, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love." (Exodus 34:6) It is the very thing Jonah complained about when grace went to a city he hated: "I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love." (Jonah 4:2) The reason the door is open is not that the Day is less terrible. The Day is exactly as terrible as Joel said. The reason the door is open is that the Judge standing at the end of it is this God, slow to anger, abounding in love, the One Hosea called the people back to with the promise that "he has torn us, that he may heal us" (Hosea 6:1). And so the prophet ends not with strategy but with the priests in tears between the porch and the altar, pleading: "Spare your people, O LORD." (Joel 2:17) The whole hope of a nation hangs on a God who might relent, and on a heart actually torn open before him.

This is where it stops being ancient. The Day of the LORD did not stay in Joel's future. It came down on a hill outside Jerusalem and landed, in full, on one man. The wrath no human strength survives, the darkness and gloom Zephaniah named, fell on Christ, so that the door God held open in Joel was finally nailed open in the cross. The torn heart God asked for, God provided, because his own heart was torn first. We do not return to a God who waits with arms crossed. We return to a God who already ran the whole length of the Day to meet us. The trumpet still sounds. The Day is still real. But the One at the end of it has a wounded side and an open door, and he is the one telling us to come home.

Rend your heart, not your clothes.

## The Years the Locust Ate
*The God who is jealous for a wrecked field, and pours himself out on everyone*

**Text:** Joel 2:18-32 · **Supporting:** Numbers 11:29 · Ezekiel 36:26-27 · Acts 2:16-21 · Isaiah 44:3

There are losses that cannot be undone. The year the marriage ended. The decade the addiction stole. The season you were too broken to be present for your own children. Joel stands in front of a field locusts ate down to the dirt and says a sentence no human being can say to those years, and means it.

**A God Who Takes It Personally**
The whole book turns on a single verse, and the hinge is jealousy. "Then the LORD became jealous for his land and had pity on his people." (Joel 2:18) The people returned, and God's response is not cool acceptance but fierce, personal possessiveness for his own. This is his land. This is his people. The locust did not merely damage a harvest; it touched what belongs to God, and God will not have it. The promise comes pouring out: "Behold, I am sending to you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be satisfied." (Joel 2:19) The empty altar of chapter one, grain and drink offering cut off, is refilled by the very hand that emptied it. "Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things." (Joel 2:21) The threshing floors fill with grain, the vats overflow with wine and oil, and God even drives back the army that did the damage: "I will remove the northerner far from you." (Joel 2:20) The exact things the locust ate are the exact things God names as he restores them. He does not give a generic comfort. He reverses the specific loss.

We assume God is detached about our ruin. Joel says he is jealous over it, and that jealousy is our only real hope.

**The Sentence No One Else Can Say**
Then comes the line that has carried more grieving people than perhaps any other in the Minor Prophets. "I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopping locust, the destroyer, and the cutting locust, my great army, which I sent among you." (Joel 2:25) Read it slowly and notice what God claims. First, he restores years, not just fields. Time itself, the thing no human power touches, the lost seasons, the wasted stretch. You can replant a field in one spring. You cannot replant a decade. Second, he names the army as his own, "my great army, which I sent." The God who restores is the God who sent the locust in the first place. This is not luck reversing course. This is the sovereign hand that wounded now choosing to heal. And the goal is not full barns but a known God: "You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God... And my people shall never again be put to shame." (Joel 2:26)

I have written years off as gone. I have looked at seasons of my own faithlessness and decided they were simply lost, subtracted from the total, never coming back. And I have counseled people to make their peace with the same arithmetic. Joel breaks the arithmetic. The God of the bare field does not merely move us forward from the ruin. He goes back into it. He restores the eaten years. That is not a thing time does. That is a thing only God does.

**Poured Out on All Flesh**
But God is not finished, and the restoration does not stop at the threshing floor. It overflows into something the world had never seen. "And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Even on the male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit." (Joel 2:28-29) Read the list and see what falls. Sons and daughters, not just sons. Old and young. Male and female servants, the bottom of the social order, the ones who owned nothing and were owned. The Spirit that once rested on a prophet here, a king there, is now poured out on all flesh, and the whole hierarchy of who gets to hear from God collapses. Moses had longed for exactly this and could only wish it: "Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!" (Numbers 11:29) Ezekiel had been promised the mechanism: "I will give you a new heart... And I will put my Spirit within you." (Ezekiel 36:26-27) Joel announces the day it floods the whole people.

And then we know exactly when that day arrived, because a fisherman stood up in Jerusalem and told us. When the Spirit fell at Pentecost and the crowd accused the disciples of being drunk, Peter answered with this chapter: "This is what was uttered through the prophet Joel: And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh." (Acts 2:16-17) The restoration Joel promised a wrecked agricultural nation found its fullness not in better harvests but in the outpoured Spirit of the risen Christ, given to sons and daughters and servants and strangers alike, given to the very people the world had written off. The God who restores the eaten years does it, finally, by pouring himself into us. And the chapter ends on the promise Peter would not stop short of: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved." (Joel 2:32) The same God who is jealous for a ruined field is jealous enough for ruined people to send his Spirit and open the door to everyone who calls.

He restores the eaten years.

## The Valley of Decision and the Refuge
*The same Day that terrifies the guilty is shelter for those who called on his name*

**Text:** Joel 3:1-21 · **Supporting:** Joel 2:32 · Obadiah 1:15 · Isaiah 2:4 · Revelation 21:3

There is a multitude in a valley, and they are waiting on a verdict. Joel calls it the valley of decision, and the decision is not theirs to make. It has already been made about them.

**The God Who Keeps the Account**
Chapter three opens with God taking up a case on behalf of people who could not defend themselves. "For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. And I will enter into judgment with them there, on behalf of my people and my heritage Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations." (Joel 3:1-2) The name Jehoshaphat means the LORD judges, the place is the verdict. And the charge sheet is specific and brutal: "they have cast lots for my people, and have traded a boy for a prostitute, and have sold a girl for wine and have drunk it." (Joel 3:3) A child reduced to the price of an afternoon's pleasure. God names it. He has not forgotten a single transaction, a single name sold, a single lot cast over a human life. He charges Tyre and Sidon and Philistia by name for taking his silver and his gold and his people. "Swiftly and speedily I will return your deeds upon your own heads." (Joel 3:7) This is the principle the prophets held without flinching, Obadiah said it plainly: "As you have done, it shall be done to you; your deeds shall return on your own head." (Obadiah 1:15) The God of Joel keeps the account of what was done to the helpless, and the account comes due.

We prefer a God too gentle to judge. But a God who will not judge what was done to that trafficked child is not gentle. He is indifferent. And the people in the valley are not afraid of an indifferent God.

**The Valley of Decision**
The prophet pulls the camera back to the whole earth and the scene becomes terrible. "Proclaim this among the nations: Consecrate for war... Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears." (Joel 3:9-10) Read that twice, because it is the famous prophecy run backward. Isaiah promised a day when nations "shall beat their swords into plowshares" (Isaiah 2:4), Joel shows the nations that refused that day melting their farm tools into weapons for a war they cannot win. "Multitudes, multitudes, in the valley of decision! For the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision." (Joel 3:14) And the cosmos itself goes dark: "The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining." (Joel 3:15) The harvest imagery turns to judgment, "Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe... for their evil is great." (Joel 3:13) The same Day of the LORD that ran through the whole book, the locust, the army, the trumpet, arrives at last as the final accounting of the nations. It is great and very awesome, and for the guilty multitude in that valley there is no door.

And I have to stand inside this and not above it, because I am capable of being the nation in the valley. I have looked away from the trafficked and the discarded and called it prudence. I have profited, in a thousand quiet ways, from systems that trade a girl for wine, and I have not lost sleep over it. The valley of decision is not only for the obvious villains of history. It is for everyone who learned to live comfortably beside an injustice God never stopped seeing.

**The Same Day, the Other Side**
Here is the turn the whole book has been building toward. In the very same paragraph, in the very same Day, two things happen at once. "The LORD roars from Zion, and utters his voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth quake." (Joel 3:16) For the nations in the valley, that roar is the end. And then, without a pause: "But the LORD is a refuge to his people, a stronghold to the people of Israel." (Joel 3:16) The same voice that shakes the earth is the shelter his people run into. The same Day that is terror for the guilty is refuge for those who called on his name back in chapter two, "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved" (Joel 2:32). The Judge and the refuge are not two beings. They are one God, and which one you meet depends entirely on whether you came home through the door he opened.

What makes the difference is not that the sheltered people were innocent. They were the same ruined nation the locust ate in chapter one. The difference is that they returned, and they called on his name, and the Spirit was poured out on them, the very Spirit Christ poured out at Pentecost on sons and daughters and servants and strangers. The refuge is not earned by clean hands. It is entered by a torn heart that ran to the only God who is both perfectly just and perfectly merciful, just enough to settle the account of every trafficked child, merciful enough to be a stronghold for sinners who came home. And the book that began with an empty altar ends with God himself moving in to stay: "the LORD dwells in Zion." (Joel 3:21) That is the last word of Joel, and it is the last word of the whole Scripture, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man." (Revelation 21:3) The Day comes for everyone. The only question Joel leaves in your hands is which God you will meet when it does.

The Judge is also the refuge.
